newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CITIC unveils five year plan, sees profits up.
newsitem.headline: CITIC unveils five year plan, sees profits up.

text.p: China International Trust & Investment Corp (CITIC), the investment arm of China's State Council, plans to focus on five core sectors and gradually diversify unrelated interests over the next five years.

"We've decided our main focuses are telecommunications, raw materials, infrastructure and trucks rather than other sectors," CITIC president Qin Xiao told a small news briefing ahead of an international trade conference in Australia.
"We are gradually selling down some other interests," he added.

He said the massive conglomerate, which had total assets of about 170 billion yuan at the end of 1995, would also concentrate on its banks, China-based CITIC Industrial Bank and Hong Kong-listed Ka Wah Bank Ltd.

"We still describe ourselves as a financial institution. Our major assets are still the banks. These banks are both sound banks, but there are a little bit too small, (they) need to grow up," Xiao said.
"In the next five years we'll put emphasis on these two banks and other non-bank financial business such as securities or even insurance."
CITIC, which has 31 subsidiaries, including six overseas, had become too diversified, a problem symptomatic of its rapid growth over the 17 years since its creation, Xiao said.
"We think we must focus on certain sectors to reconsolidate our interests. That's a big job for us over the next five years," he said.
The president said the group would be able to toast its five-year plan with at least 25 to 30 percent profit growth in calendar 1996.
"(It was) a very good year...a better year for us, at least 25 to 30 percent increase in net profit," Xiao said.
CITIC made group profits of 2.05 billion yuan last year.
The profits will go some way to help CITIC fund a major push into the Chinese telecommunications market, a sector which Xiao says shows the greatest growth potential in China.
"If you single out one sector which stands as the biggest market in China, that's telecommunications. The market is huge, particularly in the countryside," Xiao said.
The group would need to invest a total of about two billion yuan in its four Chinese telecommunications markets in order to break even, Xiao said.
"The first stage would be four cities. I think the break-even point for each city would be about 150,000 customers and that takes something like 500 million Chinese yuan (per city)," he said.
Xiao said the group's telecommunications strategy in China centered on building cellular mobile telephone services in the cities of Tianjin, Xian, Wuhan and Shenyang.

CITIC holds a telecommunications licence in the cities by virtue of its investment along with seven other Chinese companies in China's state-run telecommunications competitor China United Telecommunications (Unicom).

The president said friction between CITIC and the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications, whose China Telecom dominates wireless communications in the country, remained the key impediment to its telecommunications endeavours.
